name: Cortexin

lead: Cortexin is a peptide complex made from cattle brain cortex and prescribed in Russia and nearby countries for neurological conditions. Biohackers list it as a nootropic-style option for cognition and general wellbeing; it is not a cosmetic product.

The chain runs from a neuroprotective peptide mixture to neurological support to cognition and wellbeing. A rat study found protective effects in brain ischemia models, and a Russian randomized study looked at chronic cerebral ischemia. No appearance use is documented.

paras: In Russia it is given as a prescribed course of injections for neurological conditions. Outside that setting, it appears in biohacking lists as a periodic course.
The sources reviewed give limited safety information. It is an animal-derived injectable available by prescription in Russia and not approved in most countries.

angle.text: Cortexin is a cattle-brain peptide medicine used mainly in Russia for neurological conditions and listed by biohackers as a nootropic-style option. Local trials address neurology; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Cortexin is a neuroprotective peptide medicine made by the Russian company Geropharm from the cerebral cortex of cattle. It is given by intramuscular injection and used mainly in Russia and some post-Soviet countries for neurological conditions such as cerebrovascular disorders, head injury effects, encephalopathies and developmental delay in children.[1]

A rat study found neuroprotective activity in models of brain ischemia, and a Russian multicenter randomized study examined dose-dependent effects in chronic cerebral ischemia.[2][3] Cochrane's review of the related product Cerebrolysin, not Cortexin, addresses acute stroke.[4] No evidence was found of any appearance use; it is sometimes discussed as a nootropic.
infobox: Prescription drug in Russia; not approved in US/EU in sources reviewed

paras: Grokipedia describes Cortexin as a lyophilisate of low-molecular water-soluble polypeptide fractions from bovine cerebral cortex, with molecular weights of 1 to 10 kDa.[1] A Russian review describes it as an animal cortex extract containing neuropeptides, amino acids and trace elements.[5]

The Russian review proposes that its components act on molecular targets in neuronal signaling at several stages of pathology.[5] Grokipedia lists neuroprotective, neurotrophic and neuronal-function-restoring actions, including effects on antioxidant systems and neurotrophic factors; this is AI-generated and unverified.[1]

A multicenter randomized controlled study published in a Russian journal in 2018 examined dose-dependent effects of Cortexin in chronic cerebral ischemia.[3] No trials for appearance outcomes were found. Studies of related products exist: a Cochrane review of Cerebrolysin in acute ischaemic stroke,[4] and a blinded comparison of Cerebrolysin and other peptide preparations in embolic stroke.[6]
A 2021 PLoS ONE study compared Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and Actovegin in rat models of acute and chronic brain ischemia over 10 days, the first comparison of the three.[2]
